132 Long Discourses of the Buddha: Section on the Code of Conduct — The Discourse on the Fruits of the Contemplative Life <note>original: "Dīghanikāye Sīlakkhandhavaggo Sāmaññaphalasuttaṃ"</note>

In this way, Great King, the monk drenching, soaking, filling, and pervading this very body with a happiness that is free from physical rapture <note>the original term "tipatitakena sukhena" refers to the refined pleasure of the Third Jhana</note>. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this happiness.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the contemplative life.

68. Furthermore, Great King, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and remains in the fourth <term>jhana</term> <gloss>state of deep meditative absorption</gloss>, which is beyond pleasure and pain and purified by equanimity and mindfulness. He sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this pure, bright mind.

Great King, it is just as if a man were sitting wrapped from head to foot in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his entire body not covered by that white cloth. In the same way, Great King, the monk sits pervading this very body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of his entire body that is not pervaded by this pure, bright mind.

This, Great King, is a fruit of the contemplative life, visible here and now, more excellent and sublime than the previous fruits of the contemplative life.

69. Furthermore, Great King, when the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, the monk directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision <note>original: "ñāṇadassana"</note>. He understands this: "This is my body, possessed of form, composed of the four great elements <note>earth, water, fire, and air</note>, born of mother and father, nourished by rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, rubbing, pressing, breaking, and dissolution. And this is my <term>viññāṇa</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss>, which is fixed here and bound up with it."

70. Great King, it is just as if there were a beautiful beryl gem <note>original: "maṇi veḷuriyo"</note>, naturally pure, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. And through it was strung a thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown. A man with good sight, taking it in his hand, would reflect: "This is a beautiful beryl gem, naturally pure, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, bright, flawless, and endowed with every good quality. And through it is strung this thread—blue, yellow, red, white, or light brown."

<summary>This page describes the attainment of the fourth jhana and the subsequent development of insight into the relationship between the physical body and consciousness. It uses the metaphor of a threaded gem to illustrate how a concentrated mind perceives the connection between the material body and the spirit.</summary>

<keywords>fourth jhana, equanimity, mindfulness, consciousness, beryl gem metaphor, four elements, insight, fruits of the contemplative life</keywords>
